topic: Decoding Epidemics: The SIR Model Mechanics
target_audience: University Students (Introductory Data Science or Biology)

sections.title: Hook: The Problem of Prediction
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of predicting how a virus spreads in a population. Define the necessity of modeling to inform public health decisions.
sections.example: A single sneeze in a crowded subway car—how does that translate into thousands of cases?

sections.title: Core Components: Defining S, I, and R
sections.content: Break down the three compartments: Susceptible (can catch it), Infectious (has it), and Recovered/Removed (immune or deceased). Use a visual flow diagram of nodes moving from one bucket to another.
sections.example: Representing students as colored dots: Blue (Susceptible), Red (Infectious), and Green (Recovered).

sections.title: The Engine: Mathematical Transition Rules
sections.content: Explain the interaction between S and I (transmission rate β) and I to R (recovery rate γ). Use a graphical representation of two differential equations showing how the slopes of the curves interact.
sections.example: An animation showing Red dots bumping into Blue dots turning them Red, while Red dots slowly transition to Green over time.

sections.title: Simulation: Visualizing the Curves
sections.content: Show the classic 'Epidemic Curve.' Explain the 'Peak' and the concept of 'Flattening the Curve' by adjusting the parameters β and γ visually.
sections.example: Comparing a 'High Peak' scenario (uncontrolled) vs. a 'Flattened Curve' (social distancing/masks) through side-by-side graph animation.

sections.title: Conclusion & Real-world Application
sections.content: Summarize how simple rules create complex population behavior. Mention limitations of SIR (e.g., population mixing) and encourage further exploration of SEIR models.
sections.example: Using the model to predict herd immunity thresholds for a hypothetical animal population outbreak in a nature reserve.
